description: Foundations of reasoning and number: logic, proof, sets, numbers, pi, imaginary numbers, paradox, falsifiability, abstraction, and causality, each in four layers.

depth.picture: The rules for what follows from what.
depth.mechanism: A logic fixes a language of statements and rules for reasoning. Propositional logic combines true-or-false statements with and, or, not, and implies; predicate logic adds for all and there exists over objects and relations. An argument is valid if the conclusion must be true whenever the premises are, whatever the words mean.
depth.detail:
Aristotle's syllogisms (all humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal) were the first system, followed by the Stoics' propositional logic. Boole in 1847 turned reasoning into algebra on 0 and 1, Frege in 1879 created modern predicate logic, and Russell and Whitehead tried to found mathematics on it. Gödel proved that any consistent system rich enough for arithmetic is incomplete, and Turing and Church tied logic to computation.

Truth tables, natural deduction, and semantic tableaux are ways of checking validity. Logic is the basis of circuit design (AND, OR, and NOT gates), programming (conditions and types), databases (SQL's WHERE clauses), and automated theorem provers and SAT solvers. Non-classical logics relax classical assumptions: intuitionistic (no law of excluded middle), modal (necessity and possibility), fuzzy (degrees of truth), and paraconsistent (tolerating contradiction). Everyday reasoning departs from logic in systematic ways, as in the Wason selection task, which most people fail.
depth.principles: Logic is the study of what makes an argument compelling regardless of its subject. It is a small set of rules that turned out to be enough to build proofs, circuits, and programs.

example.label: Truth tables and two laws
example.code:
from itertools import product

def truth_table(expr, names):
    for values in product([False, True], repeat=len(names)):
        env = dict(zip(names, values))
        print(" ".join(f"{n}={int(v)}" for n, v in env.items()), "->", int(expr(**env)))

implies = lambda a, b: (not a) or b
print("P implies Q:")
truth_table(lambda P, Q: implies(P, Q), ["P", "Q"])

print(all((not (p and q)) == ((not p) or (not q)) for p, q in product([False, True], repeat=2)))   # de Morgan's law
print(all(q for p, q in product([False, True], repeat=2) if p and implies(p, q)))                  # modus ponens is valid

depth.picture: A chain of steps, each forced by the last, that leaves no room for doubt.
depth.mechanism: Start from axioms or already-proved statements, apply rules of inference, and reach the conclusion. Common methods: direct proof, contradiction (assume the opposite and derive an absurdity), induction (prove a base case and a step from n to n + 1), contrapositive, cases, and construction.
depth.detail:
Euclid's Elements, around 300 BCE, set the model: definitions, postulates, and theorems, each deduced from the previous. Example: the square root of 2 is irrational. Suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms; then a² = 2b², so a is even, a = 2c, so b² = 2c², so b is even too, contradicting lowest terms. Induction shows that 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2: it holds for n = 1, and if it holds for n it holds for n + 1.

A proof convinces because anyone can check each step. Formal proofs checked by computer (Coq, Lean, Isabelle) have verified the four-color theorem, Kepler's conjecture, and the seL4 kernel. Some proofs are enormous: the classification of finite simple groups spans tens of thousands of pages. Gödel's theorems show that some true statements cannot be proved within a given system. Evidence is not proof: a pattern verified for a trillion cases is still a conjecture, and Euler's polynomial n² + n + 41 gives primes for 40 values and then fails.
depth.principles: A proof is the one kind of evidence that never has to be revised. It is also a social act: its power comes from being checkable by anyone, which is why mathematics can build tall structures on it.

example.label: Checking is not proving
example.code:
# Induction proves 1 + 2 + ... + n = n(n+1)/2 for every n. A computer can only check cases.
print(all(sum(range(1, n + 1)) == n * (n + 1) // 2 for n in range(1, 10_000)))

is_prime = lambda k: k > 1 and all(k % d for d in range(2, int(k ** 0.5) + 1))
values = [n * n + n + 41 for n in range(45)]
print([n for n, v in enumerate(values) if not is_prime(v)])       # [40, 41, ...]: Euler's polynomial breaks at n = 40

depth.picture: Mathematics built from collections of things.
depth.mechanism: A set is a collection of distinct objects, defined by what belongs to it. From membership alone you can build subsets, unions, intersections, complements, ordered pairs, functions (sets of pairs), numbers (0 is the empty set, 1 is {0}, 2 is {0, 1}, and so on), and infinities of different sizes.
depth.detail:
Cantor created it in the 1870s, showing that the real numbers cannot be listed against the whole numbers: some infinities are larger than others, by his diagonal argument. Paradoxes followed: Russell's set of all sets that do not contain themselves both is and is not a member of itself, which forced an axiomatization. Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory with the axiom of choice (ZFC) is the standard foundation, in which nearly all of mathematics can be expressed.

The continuum hypothesis, that no infinity lies between the whole numbers and the reals, is independent of ZFC: it can be neither proved nor refuted, by Gödel in 1940 and Cohen in 1963. In practice sets appear as data types (a collection with no duplicates), in databases (tables as sets of rows), in probability (events are sets), and in logic (a predicate defines a set). Cardinality measures size: finite sets by counting, infinite ones by matching one to one.
depth.principles: One idea, collecting things, is enough to found all of mathematics. Cantor's discovery that infinity comes in sizes, and Russell's paradox, showed how much lies inside that simple idea.

example.label: Set operations, and numbers from nothing

depth.picture: Counting, then a series of inventions to answer questions counting could not.
depth.mechanism: Natural numbers (1, 2, 3, …) count. Adding zero and negatives gives the integers, so subtraction always works. Fractions (rationals) make division work. Irrationals (√2, π) fill the gaps on the number line, giving the reals. Complex numbers add √−1, so every polynomial equation has solutions.
depth.detail:
Each extension answered a question the previous system could not: 3 − 5? negative numbers. 1 ÷ 3? fractions. The diagonal of a unit square? irrational numbers, which the Pythagoreans reportedly found alarming. x² = −1? imaginary numbers. Zero as a number with its own arithmetic was developed in India (Brahmagupta, 628 CE) and reached Europe through Arabic mathematics, along with the decimal place-value system.

Kinds: primes, even and odd, squares, algebraic numbers (roots of polynomials) and transcendental ones (π, e). Cantor showed the reals cannot be listed, while the rationals can. Representation matters: Roman numerals resisted arithmetic; positional systems make it routine. Computers approximate: integers are exact but bounded, or arbitrary-precision, while floating-point reals are approximate: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3. Number theory studies whole numbers and remains full of simple unsolved questions such as Goldbach's conjecture and twin primes.
depth.principles: Each new kind of number was invented because the old ones could not answer a question that mattered. The history is a reminder that mathematics grows by demanding that operations always work.

example.label: Exact and approximate numbers
example.code:
from fractions import Fraction
import math

print(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, 0.1 + 0.2)                            # False 0.30000000000000004: floats are approximate
print(Fraction(1, 10) + Fraction(2, 10) == Fraction(3, 10))    # True: rationals are exact
print(math.sqrt(2) ** 2 == 2, round(math.sqrt(2) ** 2, 12))    # the irrational root of two, never exactly
print((-1) ** 0.5, complex(0, 1) ** 2)                         # imaginary numbers appear when you ask for root of -1
print(2 ** 200)                                                # Python integers never overflow

depth.picture: The ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, about 3.14159.
depth.mechanism: π is circumference divided by diameter, the same for every circle. It is irrational, its decimal expansion never repeating or ending, and transcendental, not the root of any polynomial with integer coefficients, so squaring the circle with ruler and compass is impossible.
depth.detail:
Ancient estimates: the Babylonians used 3.125, the Egyptians about 3.16, Archimedes bounded it between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7 with 96-sided polygons, and Zu Chongzhi in the fifth century found 355/113, accurate to six places. The symbol π was popularized by Euler in 1737. Lambert proved irrationality in 1761 and Lindemann transcendence in 1882.

Formulas include Leibniz's 1 − 1/3 + 1/5 − … = π/4, Wallis's product, Machin's arctangent formulas, Ramanujan's rapidly convergent series, and the Chudnovsky algorithm behind record computations of over 100 trillion digits. It appears far from circles: in the normal distribution, in the probability that two random integers are coprime (6/π²), in Buffon's needle problem, in Fourier analysis, and in Euler's identity. About 40 digits suffice to compute the circumference of the observable universe to the width of a hydrogen atom. Whether its digits are normal, all digit sequences equally frequent, is unproven.
depth.principles: A single number that keeps turning up wherever circles, waves, or randomness are involved. Its endless, patternless digits show how simple geometry can lead straight into the infinite.

example.label: Four ways to catch pi
example.code:
import math, random

print(355 / 113, math.pi)                                                            # Zu Chongzhi's fraction: 6 digits right
print(round(4 * sum((-1) ** k / (2 * k + 1) for k in range(1_000_000)), 5))            # Leibniz series

random.seed(71)
n = 400_000
inside = sum(random.random() ** 2 + random.random() ** 2 <= 1 for _ in range(n))
print(round(4 * inside / n, 3))                                                      # Monte Carlo darts

pairs = sum(math.gcd(random.randrange(1, 10**6), random.randrange(1, 10**6)) == 1 for _ in range(200_000))
print(round(pairs / 200_000, 3), round(6 / math.pi ** 2, 3))                          # the chance two integers are coprime

depth.picture: A number whose square is negative one, and a plane of numbers built on it.
depth.mechanism: Define i by i² = −1. A complex number is a + bi, with real part a and imaginary part b, drawn as the point (a, b) in a plane. Add componentwise; multiply by expanding and using i² = −1. Multiplying by a number of length 1 at angle θ rotates by θ.
depth.detail:
Cardano met square roots of negatives in 1545 while solving cubic equations, where they appear as intermediate steps even when all three roots are real, and Bombelli set out rules for them in 1572. Descartes called them imaginary as an insult; Gauss argued for the complex plane, and the fundamental theorem of algebra says every polynomial of degree n has exactly n complex roots. Polar form re^(iθ) links them to exponentials and trigonometry.

They are essential: alternating-current circuits use complex impedance, quantum mechanics is written with complex wave functions, signal processing uses the Fourier transform, and the Mandelbrot set lives in the complex plane. Hamilton's quaternions extend them for 3-D rotations, used in graphics and aerospace. Complex analysis is unusually rigid and powerful: a function differentiable once is infinitely differentiable. Imaginary is a poor name: they are as real as any mathematical object, and the physical world computes with them.
depth.principles: Numbers that do not sit on the number line turned out to be necessary for describing rotation, oscillation, and quantum states. Their story is the clearest case of a definition made for convenience that later turned out to describe the world.

example.label: Arithmetic, roots of unity, and rotation
example.code:
import cmath, math

z, w = 3 + 4j, 1 - 2j
print(z + w, z * w, abs(z), cmath.phase(z))                # arithmetic, the length 5.0, and the angle
print((1j) ** 2, cmath.exp(1j * math.pi))                  # i^2 = -1; Euler's identity: about -1

roots = [cmath.exp(2j * math.pi * k / 5) for k in range(5)]        # the five solutions of z^5 = 1
print([round(abs(r ** 5 - 1), 12) for r in roots])
print(round(abs((1 + 2j) * cmath.exp(1j * math.pi / 2) - (-2 + 1j)), 12))   # multiplying by i rotates a quarter turn

depth.picture: An argument that looks sound and ends in a contradiction.
depth.mechanism: Three kinds: veridical paradoxes, whose surprising conclusion is true (the birthday problem); falsidical ones, where a hidden flaw in the reasoning gives a false conclusion (the proof that 1 = 2 by dividing by zero); and antinomies, genuine contradictions that expose a flaw in our concepts and force revision, such as Russell's paradox.
depth.detail:
Zeno's paradoxes were resolved with limits and convergent series two thousand years later. The liar, this statement is false, led Tarski to show that truth for a language cannot be defined within it, and inspired Gödel's incompleteness theorems. Russell's paradox undermined naive set theory and led to axiomatic set theory and type theory. The sorites paradox, that removing one grain from a heap leaves a heap, so a single grain is a heap, exposes vagueness and motivates fuzzy logic. The barber who shaves exactly those who do not shave themselves is Russell's paradox as a story.

The ship of Theseus asks about identity through change. In decision theory, Newcomb's paradox and the prisoner's dilemma show how rationality can seem to conflict. Each paradox marks an assumption to give up: unrestricted comprehension, that truth is definable, that every predicate is sharp. Resolving them has repeatedly forced mathematics and philosophy to grow.
depth.principles: A paradox is a signpost to a hidden assumption. Many of the deepest advances, from limits to set theory to computability, came from refusing to accept an argument that seemed sound and ended in absurdity.

example.label: Russell's paradox in code, and a sharp heap

depth.picture: A claim is scientific if some possible observation could show it false.
depth.mechanism: Karl Popper proposed falsifiability in 1934 as the mark of science: a hypothesis must forbid something. All swans are white is falsifiable by a single black swan; the universe is controlled by an undetectable spirit forbids nothing. Theories gain credit by surviving serious attempts to refute them.
depth.detail:
Popper had in mind the contrast between Einstein's general relativity, which risked refutation by predicting the bending of starlight measured in 1919, and theories such as astrology, psychoanalysis, and some readings of Marxist history, which could accommodate any outcome. Strengths: it demands testable predictions and makes precision valuable, since a bold claim is more informative.

Criticisms: falsifying a single hypothesis is never clean, since tests rest on auxiliary assumptions (Duhem and Quine: an anomaly can be blamed on the instruments or on background theory; the faster-than-light neutrino result of 2011 came from a loose cable). Kuhn showed scientists stick with theories despite anomalies until a better one arrives, and probabilistic claims are never strictly falsified by one result, so statistics stands in. Still, it is a good rule of thumb: ask what would change your mind? Unfalsifiable claims are not thereby false, but they cannot be tested. Pre-registering predictions and seeking disconfirming evidence build falsifiability into research.
depth.principles: A claim that could not be wrong cannot tell you anything. Falsifiability is the discipline of asking what would count against an idea, and being willing to accept it when it happens.

depth.picture: Ignoring detail to see what is common.
depth.mechanism: Group things by shared features and give the group a name, discarding the differences that do not matter for the purpose: dog ignores breed, number ignores what is counted. In programming, an abstraction hides how something works behind an interface: you use a file, not disk sectors.
depth.detail:
Levels of abstraction stack: transistors, logic gates, processors, machine code, assembly, high-level languages, libraries, and applications, each hiding the level below. Mathematics abstracts from counting apples to numbers, from numbers to algebra, and to groups and categories. A good abstraction simplifies without lying in the cases you care about, and its interface is small.

Abstractions can leak: TCP hides packet loss until the network fails and latency shows through; garbage collection hides memory until pauses appear. Tools include functions, types, classes, modules, protocols, and APIs. Costs are indirection and overhead, and overly general abstractions that are harder to understand than the code they replace. Abstraction hides how; generalization extends to more cases. It also underlies concepts, language, and science: a word applies to many particulars, and a map abstracts a territory. Dijkstra's point was that the purpose of abstracting is not to be vague but to create a new level at which one can be precise.
depth.principles: Thinking well is choosing what to forget. An abstraction earns its place when the details it hides are exactly the ones you can afford not to know, and it fails when they turn out to matter.

example.label: Two implementations behind one interface

depth.picture: Things happen because of other things.
depth.mechanism: A causes B when making A happen, or not happen, changes whether B happens: a difference-making relation. Causes precede effects, and causal claims support counterfactuals (had the glass not fallen, it would not have broken) and interventions (if I set this, that will follow).
depth.detail:
Aristotle distinguished four causes: material, formal, efficient, and final. Hume argued we never observe causation, only constant conjunction, and infer the rest by habit. Modern accounts include counterfactual (Lewis), interventionist and graphical (Pearl, Woodward), probabilistic (causes raise probabilities), and mechanistic (identify the parts and processes).

In physics, fundamental laws are mostly time-symmetric and do not distinguish cause from effect; the direction of causation is tied to the arrow of time, entropy increase, and relativity's light cones. In science, telling correlation from cause needs randomized experiments, natural experiments, or careful modeling. Everyday causes are multiple (necessary versus sufficient, proximate versus root), and feedback loops make cause and effect run in circles, as in thermostats, ecosystems, and markets. The law's but-for test asks whether the harm would have happened without the act. Common errors are post hoc reasoning, single-cause thinking, and confusing correlation with cause.
depth.principles: Causation is what lets us act: to change things, we need to know what depends on what. It is elusive in theory and indispensable in practice, and the best tool we have for it is intervening, not just watching.

example.label: A loop where each is the cause of the other
example.code:
temp, target, heater = 15.0, 20.0, False
for minute in range(0, 61, 10):
    print(f"t={minute:2d} temp={temp:5.1f} heater={'on ' if heater else 'off'}")
    heater = temp < target                          # the temperature causes the heater's state ...
    temp += (1.2 if heater else -0.4)               # ... which causes the next temperature
